  • It has been revealed that at first glance, these shifts seem to show the success of U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that in Argentina, a giant Chinese-backed telescope project at the base of the Andes has sat partly built for more than a year, after authorities paused construction in mid-2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in Argentina, a giant Chinese-backed telescope project at the base of the Andes has sat partly built for more than a year, after authorities paused construction in mid-2025. In February, the Panamanian government ejected a subsidiary of a Hong Kong-based company from two ports on either side of the Panama Canal. And Mexico has imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on many Chinese imports since January.

It has been revealed that at first glance, these shifts seem to show the success of U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive push against Chinese influence in the Americas. His 2025 National Security Strategy pledged to “deny non-Hemispheric competitors” the ability “to own or control strategically vital assets” in the region. Allowing “incursions” by such competitors “without serious pushback is [a] great American strategic mistake of recent decades,” it added.

Recent findings suggest that in Argentina, a giant Chinese-backed telescope project at the base of the Andes has sat partly built for more than a year, after authorities paused construction in mid-2025. In February, the Panamanian government ejected a subsidiary of a Hong Kong-based firm from two ports on either side of the Panama Canal. And Mexico has imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on many Chinese imports since January.

Industry observers note that at first glance, these shifts seem to show the success of U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive push against Chinese influence in the Americas. His 2025 National Security Strategy pledged to “deny non-Hemispheric competitors” the ability “to own or control strategically vital assets” in the region. Allowing “incursions” by such competitors “without serious pushback is [a] great American strategic mistake of recent decades,” it added.

While Trump has faced resistance to his agenda in Canada and Brazil, much of the hemisphere is led by recently elected right-wing presidents who claim to be allied with Trump. It’s in many of these so-called orange-wave countries—such as Argentina and Panama—that the Trump administration’s warnings about dealings with China have appeared to lead to setbacks for high-profile Chinese investments.

But optics are not the whole story. In many Latin American countries, ties with China have continued to move forward during the Trump years, according to key metrics such as trade flows, visits by high-level officials, and public opinion surveys. Some analysts even argue that the United States’ claim to a sphere of influence in the Americas may be a strategic blunder that could benefit China.

“I think if the Americans choose the path of coercion to try to reach their goals in the region,” remarked Sebastián Hurtado of Ecuadorian consultancy Prófitas, “it’s going to backfire.”.

It has been revealed that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth (right) signs a bilateral agreement with Panama’s President Jose Raul Mulino in Panama City on April 9, 2025. Franco Brana/AFP via Getty Images.

Trump’s anti-China push in the Americas has so far targeted—or voiced aims to target—a vast swath of economic activity, including investments in ports, the oil sector, critical minerals, and communications infrastructure. U.S. officials have argued that these assets could be used for Chinese military purposes or that they are needed for U.S. security reasons.

According to recent reports, beijing has retaliated to some of these moves. After Panama’s Supreme Court booted the subsidiary of a Hong Kong-based firm out of two ports following Trump’s complaints, China upped maritime detentions of Panama-flagged ships. In Paraguay, China sanctioned a sitting government official for the first time ever: the information technology minister, after Paraguay affirmed ties with Taiwan and blocked Chinese companies from building the country’s 5G network.

Even so, it’s noteworthy that Beijing has chosen a more muted response to other aggressive U.S. moves in the region, experts say. The U.S. apprehension of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela—a country that China has dubbed an “all-weather strategic partner”—in January triggered verbal condemnations but no major retaliation. Beijing also revealed restraint after Mexico levied steep tariffs on Chinese goods following the United States’ urging.

The country’s troubling relationship to China is at the center of its presidential campaign.

Rather than pushing Beijing out of the region, Washington should offer countries better strategic alternatives.

Even the most MAGA of the region’s leaders can’t abandon their motor of economic development.

In a recent development, on Venezuela, Chinese officials “haven’t made a huge scandal, and they could have,” said Francisco Urdinez, an expert on China-Latin America relations at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. Urdinez argued that in general, “China always understood that the hemisphere is a natural sphere of influence for Washington,” adding that the United States “exerts absolute hegemony in military aspects.”.

Beijing’s core interests in the region are mostly economic—maintaining access to food and commodities exports and some big-ticket investments—as well as the fact that the region contains the largest share of countries in the world that officially recognize Taiwan, he said.

It has been revealed that many of these economic links are hard to undo because they are governed by long-term contracts. Often, there’s no easy replacement for Chinese buyers. Chile, for example, exports most of its copper and lithium to China rather than the United States in part because China has refining capacity that the United States lacks.

In a recent development, the Trump administration has generally been slow to offer Latin American countries alternatives to doing business with China. Though Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa is a vocally pro-Trump president, his country’s “trade and investment relationship with the United States is stagnant,” Hurtado remarked. Chinese trade and investment jumped after a free trade deal took effect in 2024, and Chinese demand has helped boost Ecuador’s shrimp industry to become its top export. Noboa has visited China twice during his current term.

These economic realities help explain why Beijing has sometimes chosen restraint in response to Trump’s so-called Donroe Doctrine. A “couple of wins … lets the administration maybe rest on its laurels a little bit and then get distracted from the broader economic trends that fundamentally haven’t changed,” stated Audrye Wong of the American Enterprise Institute.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (left) and China’s Great Wall Motor CEO Mu Feng (right) raise their hands during the inauguration of the GWM automobile factory in Iracemapolis, Brazil on Aug. 15, 2025.Nelson Almeida/AFP via Getty Images.

In a recent development, china might have already treated the Americas as a de facto sphere of U.S. military influence before Trump took office. But his administration’s public acknowledgement of the idea has triggered a series of debates in the Chinese, Latin American, and U.S foreign-policy communities over whether China and Latin American countries would welcome explicit spheres of influence.

While right-wing Latin American presidents have gone along with some of Trump’s priorities, especially regarding crime and immigration, they’ve shown unease with full alignment when it comes to China. Many, like Noboa, have continued robust trade with China. Brazil’s newly reelected left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, puts things more bluntly: “Dividing the world into zones of influence and making neocolonial incursions for strategic resources are anachronistic moves,” he said at the United Nations General Assembly in September.

In official statements, Beijing claims it rejects spheres of influence. But some observers of Chinese foreign policy, including Latin American officials who’ve dealt with Chinese counterparts, have argued that Beijing would be open to the idea—especially if it means the United States staying out of the Asia-Pacific. “China has no problem with the world being divided into spheres of influence” because “it reveals weakness in the idea that the U.S. is the global superpower,” said Hussein Kalout, a former senior Brazilian foreign-policy official.

“I think China would be very satisfied if the world were divided the way it is in Trump’s head,” stated Igor Patrick, the Latin America correspondent for the South China Morning Post, based in Rio de Janeiro. “But there’s an concern beyond the geopolitics of military interests, and that’s Chinese investment,” he added.

In a recent development, A construction project at the Port of Balboa, managed by CK Hutchison Holdings based in Hong Kong, at the entrance to the Panama Canal in Panama City on Feb. 23. Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that latin American and Caribbean countries have received more than $200 billion in Chinese investment since 2000, according to researchers at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Many of those investments support the flow of critical minerals back to China, like iron and copper mines, or the global sales strategy for Chinese goods, like electric car factories.

Sources indicate that but China’s economic relationships—and its economic influence—are not uniform across the region. Mexico and Central American countries like Panama remain more deeply integrated with the U.S. economy than with China. And it is there that the Trump administration has generally been more successful at pressuring Chinese business to leave. Trump has had less success in Brazil, the world’s top recipient of Chinese investment in 2025.

At a Johns Hopkins University roundtable on Chinese foreign policy earlier this year, multiple speakers brought up another obstacle to a system based on spheres of influence: Beijing does not trust the United States enough to know that any hypothetical deal to respect spheres of influence would endure.

Shiao Wang, an assistant professor at Fudan University who researches Latin America, wrote in an email that she “would be cautious about interpreting China’s responses to particular U.S. initiatives as evidence that a particular geopolitical arrangement was accepted.” She added that Latin American countries’ own economic needs help explain China’s relations in the region.

For now, rather than being traded as part of a grand bargain between the United States and China, Latin America finds itself in the middle of an uncomfortable tug-of-war.

In a recent development, demonstrators during an anti-Trump protest in Bogotá, Colombia, on Jan. 7.Andres Rot/Getty Images.

It’s unclear how much Chinese business Trump will manage to push out of Latin America during his term. But one trend is emerging: Throughout the region, public opinion of China is improving relative to that of the United States.

In a recent development, earlier this year, respondents to a Pew poll in five out of six Latin American countries stated that their views of the United States had worsened. Views of China largely remained steady. A Latinobarómetro survey found that since 2024, opinions of China have improved, and opinions of the United States have declined in 15 out of 17 Latin American countries. It was the first time that more people in the region told Latinobarómetro that China was a positive influence than was the United States.

Industry observers note that “China is not applying sanctions, going to war, or harming its friends,” Kalout noted of the shift, adding that U.S. tariffs and immigration restrictions also took a toll. Urdinez, who studies public opinion about China in the region, cautioned that it has historically been volatile. He said that China’s bump is mainly due to its contrast with Trump’s foreign policy.

According to recent reports, still, he added, China has been attracting some popularity on its own terms through the provision of high-tech goods like BYD cars, which are increasingly common in the region. “Ecuadorians view China as a country that has promptly taken off. And before, we saw the United States like that,” Hurtado said.

For Urdinez, monitoring these public opinion shifts is part of tracking a long-term influence game. Beyond the question of who controls a specific mine or port, he argued that bigger issues are at play—such as whether Latin American countries ultimately align with China’s worldview in global forums like the U.N. If they do, it suggests that China has translated its economic ties into more holistic geopolitical influence in the region, even despite the ubiquity of hard U.S. military assets.

Speaking about Brazil, Kalout said people “prefer the United States over China due to cultural relations, values, economic ties, and related secular traditions.” But whether that relationship proves more durable “depends a lot on how the United States acts in the coming decades,” he said.

Industry observers note that catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn.

Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024. Two years later, Democrat Scott Colom won the state’s Senate race, ending a Republican hold that had lasted more than four decades.

Colom’s victory was part of a string of Democratic breakthroughs during the midterms in places Trump had carried by double digits. Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina, captured the Texas governor’s office and flipped a Republican-held House seat deep in Trump country in Indiana that had not elected a Democrat since 1990.

The results stand out for more than the presidential margins as well — Democrats broke Senate streaks that had lasted decades and defeated Republican incumbents in races many expected the GOP to hold, including one where the Democratic challenger spent next to nothing on television advertisements.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE.

Here are five of the year’s most striking upsets:.

Industry observers note that democratic and Republican Party emblems are displayed with an American flag background in this photo illustration taken on Aug. 25, 2022. Democrats flipped several red-state seats during the 2026 midterm elections. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images).

Trump carried the state by nearly 23 points in 2024, and a Democrat had not won a U.S. Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. Several major election forecasters rated the contest Solid Republican for much of the cycle, before shifting it to Likely Republican as the race tightened.

In a recent development, colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., by less than one percentage point, 49.36% to 48.54%, according to Associated Press election results. Hyde-Smith had Trump’s backing, and the president rallied for her in the campaign’s final days. Meanwhile, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, made a seven-figure late-campaign ad buy, as previously reported by Fox News Digital.

It has been revealed that the Associated Press did not call the race until Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day. Colom will also become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction.

The margin was razor-thin, but the political barrier was enormous — a Trump +23 state, a Trump-backed incumbent and a 44-year drought in Democratic Senate victories. But Democrats pulled off the upset.

Scott Colom walks across the campus of Jackson State University on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, in Jackson, Miss. Colom defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, ending a 44-year Democratic Senate drought in the state. (Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images).

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, R-Texas, as he sought an unprecedented fourth term, ending a 36-year Democratic losing streak in Texas governor’s races. Trump had carried the state by 13.7 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data, and an October Fox News poll highlighted Abbott ahead leading up to the Nov. 3 election. Hinojosa, however, ultimately won with 52.8% of the vote to Abbott’s 45.7%, according to Associated Press election results.

Industry observers note that her victory was a major break from Texas’ recent political history and a miss by many major polls. It also made Hinojosa the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats had not won the governor’s office since Ann Richards’ 1990 victory.

Industry observers note that texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa speaks during a campaign rally in Austin on Nov. 2, 2026. She unseated GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

Hinojosa’s win was one of two Democratic statewide breakthroughs in Texas, as Democratic state Rep. James Talarico also defeated Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

It has been revealed that south Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998, when Fritz Hollings won his final term, and Trump carried the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data. Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician who had never held elected office before, defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, by nearly five points.

Recent findings suggest that graham had Trump’s endorsement and the president also helped her with late campaign appearances on the trail. She had been appointed to serve out her brother’s term after his death, then won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term.

Andrews’ win broke a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the state’s Senate seat and became a rare moment when a Trump-backed candidate lost in a state Republicans had long counted on.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews face off during a South Carolina U.S. Senate debate in Columbia on Oct. 11, 2026. Andrews went on to defeat Graham, ending a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the seat. (Courtesy: SCETV).

Kansas had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George McGill won a full term. Hamilton, a Democrat and the founding pastor of a large United Methodist church, defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, according to election data from the Associated Press.

The Kansas race was long viewed as a Republican hold, but major election forecasters moved it into toss-up territory late in the campaign as Marshall faced scrutiny over his residency and lawsuits his former medical practice filed against patients.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both campaigned for Marshall, and Republican-aligned groups spent heavily to keep the seat, including more than $26 million committed to ads supporting him after the August primary — more than was spent on Marshall during his first race in 2020, according to AdImpact data cited by the Associated Press.

Hamilton’s win ended a 94-year Republican Senate streak.

Sources indicate that sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., left, and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, who became the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. (Getty Images).

Democrat J.D. Ford defeated three-term Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, which Trump carried by about 17 points, according to Associated Press election results from 2024. Spartz had won re-election there by 18.6 points in 2024, and the district had not elected a Democrat since 1990, when Jim Jontz won.

Recent findings suggest that ford, a Democratic state senator, won 51.7% to Spartz’s 48.3%, according to the Associated Press results after the midterms. His victory was the only Indiana House seat to change parties, making it a sharp reversal in a state that Trump carried by 19 points statewide in 2024.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Broderick spent under $100,000 compared to DesJarlais’ more than $500,000. The Associated Press has yet to formally call the race with 99% of the vote counted so far.

Congress and the Coming Crises

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • LINDSAY is Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S.
  • Industry observers note that how to Defuse Looming Threats to U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that IVO H. DAALDER is Senior Fellow at Harvard’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs. He served as U.S. Ambassador to NATO from 2009 to 2013.

Sources indicate that JAMES M. LINDSAY is Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Industry observers note that how to Defuse Looming Threats to U.S. National Security.

Sources indicate that ivo H. Daalder and James M. Lindsay.

Democrats won a historic victory in the U.S. midterm elections by running on a key voter concern: affordability. They promised to lower gas and diesel prices, curb electricity and water bills, and cut borrowing costs. Now voters expect results.

Making progress will not be easy, given that the affordability crisis is inextricably linked to a set of thorny policy complications. Soaring gas and diesel prices stem from wars in Europe and the Middle East that have overextended the United States and provided China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia openings to exploit. Rising electricity and water bills are driven by the growing number of data centers powering an artificial intelligence revolution that is nearing a point of no return, when machines improve faster than humans can understand or control. And higher prices and borrowing costs are the result of an unsustainable U.S. national debt, now above $40 trillion, that requires exorbitant interest payments and has foreign governments questioning the safety of the dollar and U.S. Treasury bonds.

These problems not only strain Americans’ pocketbooks but also threaten the security and prosperity of the United States—and the world. If Beijing and Moscow try to take advantage of a weakened United States by escalating simultaneously in Taiwan and eastern Europe, those moves could be the first steps toward World War III. If AI escapes the bounds of human control, no one will be safe. And if the national debt continues to soar, Washington could trigger a fiscal crisis that devastates the American economy and leaves the United States far less able to meet the challenges it faces overseas.

In a recent development, action to address the United States’ problems therefore cannot wait. But politics may stand in the way. The White House is more likely to obstruct than to cooperate with congressional Democrats over the next two years, as President Donald Trump’s appointment of the pugilistic Stephen Miller as the latest White House chief of staff underscores. Moreover, one electoral victory did not erase the country’s deep partisan and policy divisions. Going into the 2028 presidential election, Republicans know that a successful Democratic Congress would endanger their chances of keeping the White House. Trump and congressional Republicans, therefore, have considerable motivation to derail Democratic plans.

Democrats are not without options, however. They can pursue legislation, seeking cross-party collaboration when possible and pushing ahead even in the face of presidential vetoes. Sometimes it is the president, not Congress, who blinks. When he doesn’t, voters will know who stood in the way. Democrats can also use public hearings and the investigative powers of Congress to shed light on the threats facing the country and to build a case for change—much as the Fulbright hearings did during the Vietnam War and the Church Committee did to highlight Cold War–era intelligence abuses. They can put the defense secretary and military commanders, AI executives, and Treasury and budget officials under oath to account for how they prosecuted the Iran war, raced ahead on AI without adequate safeguards, and exploded the deficit. They can also call on economists, scientists, and strategists to explain how to steer the country away from peril.

According to recent reports, congressional efforts may not be enough to meaningfully change Trump’s policies. But the risks of major war, unconstrained AI, and eroding economic competitiveness are too great to wait two more years to address. These problems, and the affordability crisis they have generated, will only get worse. If Democrats in Congress do not start advancing a serious agenda to address them now, these dangers may become impossible to contain.

Industry observers note that the first order of the latest Congress’s business should be to end the Iran war. Operation Epic Fury has sent energy prices soaring and put freedom of navigation at risk. It has also highlighted the United States’ vulnerabilities in ways that could prove dangerous—and costly—in the years ahead. Iranian missiles and drones wreaked havoc on American military bases in the Persian Gulf. U.S. efforts to defeat these attacks depleted supplies of critical munitions, showing that the U.S. military has become overly reliant on very expensive, hard-to-produce high-tech weapons. The economic, diplomatic, military, and intelligence support that China and Russia have provided Iran revealed the extent to which autocracies are cooperating to stretch U.S. capabilities and undermine American power. The U.S. Navy is effectively bottled up in the Arabian Sea, limiting its presence in the Atlantic and Pacific. In theory, U.S. allies could help fill the gaps, but Trump’s decision to launch the war without consulting them and his adversarial attitude toward them have strained those relationships, weakening deterrence of a Russia and China bent on securing strategic advantage.

Perceptions of weakness, even when they are wrong, are often why wars begin. Moscow and Beijing might see the next two years as a window of opportunity. Europe and Japan are rearming, but that buildup will take years. The American military is stretched thin, and political divisions make decisive action difficult. Together this could be an invitation for U.S. adversaries to engage in aggression in Europe and Asia. Russia is already pursuing a shadow war against NATO and could test the alliance’s unity further by probing the Baltic states. China could impose a blockade on Taiwan. It is not difficult to see how, if Moscow and Beijing take these steps in concert, the resulting conflicts could escalate into a global war.

Industry observers note that the latest Congress will have limited ability to forestall these events. The U.S. Constitution puts much of diplomacy beyond the reach of the legislature; only the president decides when to negotiate, what to discuss, and with whom. But Congress does have tools to wield. If the Trump administration remains in a standoff with the Iranian regime when Democrats take control in January, Congress should immediately invoke the War Powers Resolution to pass binding legislation demanding that Trump either secure congressional authorization for the war or end it. Congress can also use its power of the purse to condition or halt further spending on the war, preferably as part of must-pass legislation, such as a defense appropriations bill, to avoid a potential Senate filibuster. Trump would likely veto any such legislation, and Congress has a poor record on overriding presidential vetoes. But challenging a war that Americans clearly oppose would fulfill the promise Democrats made on the campaign trail, reduce the likelihood that Trump would escalate in dangerous ways, and mark a step forward in Congress’s reclamation of its war powers.

It has been revealed that there is more the Democratic Congress can do to lower the risks of global conflict, too. It can start by taking a stronger line on Russia. Moscow has repaid Trump’s conciliatory policies—including his waiving of sanctions Congress authorized earlier this year with the bipartisan Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act—with aid to Tehran and an intensified war on Ukraine. Only greater pressure can force the Kremlin to stand down. Congress should amend the Graham Act to give itself the right to review and overturn any presidential waivers of sanctions mandated under the law. It should also reaffirm the current ban on energy purchases from Russia and prohibit the administration from using government funds to follow through on its proposal to restart Russian gas and oil exports to Europe through a U.S. intermediary. Congress should resume military aid to Ukraine, ensure the availability of Starshield communications to Ukrainian forces, and refuse to fund any reduction in the permanent U.S. military presence in Europe or Asia that it has not approved itself.

Finally, to help dissuade China from threatening Taiwan, Congress should use defense spending bills to speed up the sale of arms to Taiwan. And Congress should legally codify the 1982 Six Assurances, which include a promise by Washington not to consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan. Many of these measures could garner sufficient Republican support to pass with veto-proof majorities, forcing Trump’s hand.

Additionally, Congress should use its oversight powers to assess the vulnerabilities that the Iran war has revealed. It should evaluate whether the U.S. intelligence agencies and the Pentagon adequately anticipated Iran’s response to U.S. attacks, the scale and causes of the shortages of high-tech weapons, and the risks that AI-aided drone warfare poses to U.S. overseas bases. Congress can also review the extent of Chinese and Russian support for Iran; assess NATO’s defenses against Russia, including its response to the escalating shadow war; determine U.S. readiness for Chinese efforts to coerce Taiwan; and evaluate proposals to make Pentagon acquisition more flexible and less expensive. An essential step toward enhancing U.S. deterrence is to identify what is broken in the U.S. defense posture and what needs to be fixed.

In a recent development, the fresh Congress will also need to rein in the AI industry. Opposition to AI data centers and other infrastructure galvanized voters in the midterms. Across the country, 46 of 47 ballot measures passed, placing new restrictions on new data centers, which have brought rising power and water bills and explosive land costs. Many Americans fear what AI will do to jobs today and for the next generation. They distrust the tech executives who control it and question who will truly benefit from its development.

Those concerns are justified. AI is advancing with increasing speed and introducing unknown risks. Five months ago, AI generated one percent of Anthropic’s research and development; today, it accounts for more than a quarter. Lab leaders predict that AI will become self-generating within a year. That is a scary prospect, not only for displaced computer scientists but also for society at large. AI could pose an existential threat to global computer networks; rogue AI agents have already colluded to evade human control. Leading firms have warned of even greater dangers. Alphabet remarked recently that its products could lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents,” and Anthropic has cited “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”.

AI also poses profound national security challenges for the United States. The Trump administration and the tech industry have invoked an innovation race with China as a reason not to regulate the technology. That race is real, but many of the most vital stages are not the ones Washington is fixating on. They are also ones Beijing is winning. Perhaps U.S. firms will be the first to develop artificial general intelligence. But in the meantime, the rest of the world and many U.S. companies are adopting Chinese open-weight AI models. Alibaba’s Qwen model now accounts for more than half of all open-source model downloads worldwide. As cheap, easy-to-adapt Chinese models become the global default, Beijing gains leverage over the digital infrastructure on which other countries’ economies and militaries will run. The companies that build these models are legally bound to cooperate with Chinese intelligence services. And because these models spread with few safeguards, they are easier to turn to malicious use.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, AI is transforming war. Autonomous weapons are essential to Ukraine’s defense against a superior military, shooting down long-range drones and targeting Russian forces, supply lines, and strategic industries. This year, the Pentagon quietly revised its doctrine to let AI select and initiate strikes while humans merely monitor, which risks errors and escalation at a speed no human can catch. And as AI lowers the barriers to entry for launching cyberattacks and developing fresh biological weapons, every country is in danger.

According to recent reports, the Trump administration is clearly reluctant to address any of these threats. It is beholden to figures such as Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerburg who have wanted to keep the AI industry unregulated and unconstrained. Huang and Nvidia, the tech giant he led, had long pushed the administration to relax U.S. export controls that restricted the sale of AI chips to China and other countries; the firm’s current scandal has revealed just how loose those restrictions had become. Now, the administration wants China to report serious AI-related incidents through a new bilateral channel yet opposes requiring American companies to do the same. Given how rapidly AI is advancing, Congress cannot afford to stand idly by. There is a slew of legislative proposals already circulating, many of them with bipartisan support, that would require incident reporting, auditors in AI labs, and mandatory safety testing before deployment. Other AI industry leaders, such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis, have supported these ideas, but the Trump administration has ignored them, asking instead for the industry to police itself.

Finding the right regulations and safety mechanisms, and then codifying them in legislation, will take time. In the meantime, Congress should use its convening power to seek input from industry leaders, experts, and the public about how this technology can be controlled. The leaders of frontier AI labs should be asked, under oath, to explain not just the upside of AI but also its risks. Elon Musk, for example, told The Economist this summer that within ten years, work will be “optional” because of AI—but he has also mentioned there is a ten to 20 percent chance that AI will lead to the extinction of humanity. He and others who share this belief should be forced to justify why this risk is acceptable and why tech leaders are the ones to decide on behalf of humanity. They should also explain what it would take to reduce the ten to 20 percent chance to zero.

Public hearings that expose both the dangers and the opportunities of AI will make it easier to galvanize action to harness the technology’s promise safely while preventing the worst possible outcomes. And Congress has some levers it can pull now to address threats to national security. It can use the defense authorization bill to require that humans retain meaningful control over lethal force and to demand an accounting of how AI is reshaping military doctrine. It can also fund efforts to make American models, rather than Chinese ones, the default choice for countries around the world. If legislation takes too long to pass, hearings can at least lay the groundwork for a future administration to act.

Finally, Congress must address threats to the United States’ economic power. With $40 trillion in public debt, an annual budget deficit of $2 trillion, and annual interest payments topping more than $1 trillion, the U.S. economy is living on borrowed time. China and Russia are working to “de-dollarize” their economies by encouraging the use of cryptocurrency and other means of settling international transactions and by creating alternatives to the U.S.-dominated global banking system.

Even U.S. allies are reducing their reliance on that system: Norway’s sovereign wealth fund has cut its holding of U.S. dollars, the Dutch and French central banks have pulled their gold holdings from Latest York, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has called for a “global euro” that would serve as an alternative to the dollar. If the dollar were to lose its status as the world’s premier reserve currency, Washington would be forced to spend even more money servicing the debt than it does now, intensifying the country’s fiscal problems, slowing economic growth while driving up inflation, and diminishing its ability to use economic and financial sanctions to pressure adversaries.

It has been revealed that an immediate objective for the Democratic Congress will be to rein in Trump’s tariffs, because they raise prices, unsettle the markets that finance U.S. debt, and make U.S. producers less competitive globally without making a meaningful dent in the deficit. Congress will be operating from a disadvantage. Over the past century, it has delegated to the White House considerable tariff-setting authority, which Trump has eagerly exercised. Clawing back that power will be difficult. Significant disagreement exists among Democrats and between Democrats and Republicans about how to rewrite tariff law, and Trump will likely fight to defend his favorite foreign policy tool. Yet one area where concerted congressional action might be possible is in walking back Trump’s unilateral tariffs on Canada, which not only run counter to the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement that Trump negotiated and Congress approved in his first term but also hurt Republican voters in Maine and across the Midwest. Congress can aim to repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on countries that treat U.S. goods differently from those from other countries. The provision was a forgotten relic until Trump invoked it in August to impose a fresh round of tariffs on Canada. And legislators should narrow the reach of other presidential tariff authorities by mandating expedited congressional review, instituting joint resolutions of disapproval that cannot be filibustered, and adding sunset provisions to emergency tariff authorities so that the president needs congressional approval to keep them in place.

Tariffs, however, are only part of the problem. A comprehensive solution to the country’s fiscal troubles would require raising taxes or cutting entitlements, which neither party has been willing to do. But Democrats have other cards they can play to start undoing the damage of the past two years. Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will cost the Treasury some $4.5 trillion over the next decade; Congress should repeal the law’s tax breaks for corporations and the wealthiest Americans and restore the Internal Revenue Service’s ability to collect taxes that are already owed. It should also write the Federal Reserve’s independence into law, so that no president can force interest rates down to make government borrowing cheaper. And Congress should establish a bipartisan commission modeled on the 1981 Greenspan Commission, which resolved a Social Security funding crisis, to recommend steps the United States must take to put its finances on a sustainable path and to ensure its global economic competitiveness.

In his 1948 campaign, Harry Truman salvaged his presidency by running against what he called the “do-nothing” Congress. That history should be a warning to Democrats. Voters handed them a congressional majority to bring down costs, and they must start right away to address the forces driving those costs—wars stretching American power to the breaking point, an AI revolution racing beyond human control, and a fiscal hole eroding the foundations of U.S. economic power. If the Democratic majority spends the next two years relitigating the administration’s misdeeds but failing to make progress on the issue voters care most about, Trump and the next Republican presidential candidate will be happy to brand it the do-nothing Congress of 2028.

In a recent development, passing bills that can become law, forcing the president to veto those that cannot, and using hearings to show Americans what is at stake may still fall short. Ending and averting war, regulating a powerful tech industry, and protecting the United States’ economic competitiveness are difficult for Congress to do without presidential cooperation. But two years without any progress would only leave the affordability problem in place and the United States in a more dangerous global position than it is in now. A Congress that confronts these problems directly can at least make headway. And if it does its job right, it will hand the next president an agenda equal to the moment.

Picture this: You’re curled up in your favorite chair with a cup of hot cocoa, fire crackling, Bing Crosby crooning on the stereo, and you pull out a 400-plus-page tome on the 1,000-year history of bond markets. Or the adaptability of the European Union. Or perhaps grand strategy in the Middle East. If any of these scenarios appeal to you, you’re in the right place. Below, you’ll find holiday reading recommendations from FP staff and columnists, whose 2026 picks range from wonky to contemplative to downright fun.—Chloe Hadavas.

Robin Wigglesworth (Portfolio, 416 pp., $35, September 2026).

According to recent reports, picture this: You’re curled up in your favorite chair with a cup of hot cocoa, fire crackling, Bing Crosby crooning on the stereo, and you pull out a 400-plus-page tome on the 1,000-year history of bond markets. Or the adaptability of the European Union. Or perhaps grand strategy in the Middle East. If any of these scenarios appeal to you, you’re in the right place. Below, you’ll find holiday reading recommendations from FP staff and columnists, whose 2026 picks range from wonky to contemplative to downright fun.—Chloe Hadavas.

Robin Wigglesworth (Portfolio, 416 pp., $35, September 2026).

I imagine there are likely only two reactions when readers stumble across a book such as A Fabulous Debt, a 1,000-year tale of bond market magic and mischief: Shoot me now, or straight into my veins. I’m in the latter camp, and unabashedly so. This is a fantastically entertaining read, and no holiday is complete, in our household at least, without in-depth discussions of financial crises dating back centuries.

In a recent development, robin Wigglesworth’s book is so much fun to read because it is a fast-paced, exhaustively researched history of the driest subject in the world written in the most engaging way possible. Bonds—debt that pays interest, and that finances governments and companies—are actually the secret to understanding the whims and vagaries of everything that has happened since Venice was on the upswing in the pre-Renaissance years to the latest market meltdown over U.S. President Donald Trump’s wild policies. There is literally nothing more central, and perhaps less well understood, to the world today, and Wigglesworth is the worthiest of sherpas.

Beyond all the financial innovation—which was much, and often not even criminal—the characters alone are amazing. From 12th-century Venetian doges to Alexander Hamilton to 19th-century rail barons to 1980s bond villains, and then, just a few decades later, even more creative bond villains. This is the prequel to The Big Short.

If I were a ratings agency, I would give the book an AAA+.

Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff (Harper, 256 pp., $30, April 2026).

A guide for the perplexed? I feel seen; count me in.

Sources indicate that just as there was once Fordism—the shorthand homage to Henry Ford and 20th-century capitalism that married mass production with mass consumption—our current era of bewilderment probably needed its own -ism. Enter Elon Musk. Co-authors Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff make the case that Muskism is a worldview that offers an “operating system” for our times. But you, dear reader, are not just partaking in Musk’s OS by buying his cars or renting his internet. You are becoming part of his universe. “Trying to unplug from Musk,” the book points out, “you realize he owns the socket.”.

This is a slim, urgent, and highly readable book on the man who thinks he is the world’s most important being. It is also about what Musk’s rise means for the rest of us—the permanently perplexed—whose tax dollars fueled his ambitions, who watched as he gutted the federal government, and who continue to wonder why we’re developing flying cars when all our actual flights are delayed. Mercifully, unlike some other works on Musk, this is no hagiography. Instead, it charts out how Musk came about his views and how his techno-maximalist, anti-humanitarian venom came to poison much of Silicon Valley.

Catherine E. De Vries and Alexandros Kentikelenis (Oxford University Press, 256 pp., $34.99, October 2026).

According to recent reports, who in their right mind would read a book about the European Union during a holiday? Well, think twice. How Europe Survives by Catherine E. De Vries and Alexandros Kentikelenis is one of the more upbeat books you will ever read about the subject. From their perches in Madrid and Milan, the two political scientists explain why the crises that have plagued Europe in the past two decades—such as the eurozone crisis, refugee crisis, Brexit, the war in Ukraine, and the COVID-19 pandemic—have not killed the EU, as many predicted.

In their telling, Europe is like a living mechanism. It improvises and adapts to its circumstances, albeit slowly. With each crisis, Europe’s leaders face a choice: Fall in the precipice or seek compromise. So far, they have opted for the latter. The result is often far from pretty, but as the book reminds us, these compromises generally produce a quality of life, stability, and moderation that make some other nations green with envy.

—Caroline de Gruyter, FP columnist.

Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026).

It has been revealed that it felt like the world was ending most weeks this year. “BREAKING: EVERYTHING” was a pithy summation of that time the planes were grounded and Microsoft Outlook sputtered to a halt. (I’m sure as you read this, fresh hells will have presented themselves.) Amid such systemic collapse, the concept of a dystopic sci-fi novel set in the smoldering ruins of an American civil war was not appealing—until I read a review of Exit Party that said it was “cozy.”.

In a recent development, the novel, which begins with a really bad party off the Sunset Strip in the newly formed Republic of California, courses with adrenaline but never resignation. With a dash of the Bourne movies and a soupcon of fellow Canuck Margaret Atwood, Emily St. John Mandel invokes our worst nightmares and then uses them as a mere backdrop to an absorbing story about art, friendship, and love, asking, “Who will you be at the end of the world?”.

Wil Haygood (Knopf, 384 pp., $35, February 2026).

By bringing readers deeply into the experiences of African American soldiers during the Vietnam War, Wil Haygood’s The War Within a War confronts us with the reality of the socioeconomic and racial inequality so often at the heart of modern warfare, and especially of its American variants.

Through individual stories that come to life on the page, Haygood documents how Black soldiers were disproportionately represented on the battlefield in Vietnam, and how these soldiers were disproportionately killed and wounded early in the war. Yet they were promoted to positions of command in numbers well beneath those that their presence on the front lines would have suggested. He also demonstrates the indifferent treatment that Black veterans commonly experienced upon their discharge, when many faced few options beyond returning to poverty-ravaged inner-city neighborhoods, where jobs were scarce and cheap narcotics plentiful.

Haygood’s book joins a growing literature about the bitter irony of African American soldiers fighting, from the U.S. Revolution and the Civil War to the present, for the freedom and full citizenship of others, even as they have been denied these things or discriminated against themselves.

—Howard W. French, FP columnist.

Robin Yassin-Kassab (Saqi Books, 352 pp., $27.95, September 2026).

Not long after the Syrian uprising began in 2011, I started receiving email installments of Robin Yassin-Kassab’s blog, Qunfuz. I had never heard of him, but his searing and eloquent takes on Syria ensured that I did not send Qunfuz to my junk folder. So, when I saw that Yassin-Kassab had written a book, it was an easy preorder.

It has been revealed that the Blood Between Us is not an eyewitness account. Yassin-Kassab is of Syrian and Scottish descent, lives in the United Kingdom, and only made a few relatively brief forays into Syria during its 14-year conflict. This is actually to the volume’s benefit, however. Yassin-Kassab offers both the intimacy of the bloodletting as told to him by his interlocutors and an analytic detachment that provides perspective on the Syrian revolution as it unfolded.

His central point is that the Syrian people’s triumph in December 2024 was not the bolt from the blue that it seemed. Despite the static battlefield, repression, displacement, and death, the uprising against the Assad regime never ended. Admittedly, The Blood Between Us is not an uplifting holiday read, so maybe hold off for a few weeks—but do not miss it.

Robert Jackson Bennett (Del Rey, 400 pp., $32, August 2026).

The most entertaining book I’ve read this year was Robert Jackson Bennett’s A Trade of Blood, the third in his ongoing series of fantasy detective stories. Bennett’s tales of a cantankerous master detective and her long-suffering, curious sidekick are an exercise in how to keep sequels fresh—and also examinations of the dilemmas of power and the double-sidedness of a government trying to do good things through troublesome means. They can stand with some of the best of Golden Age detective literature, but they also have giant monsters.

Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick (Atria/One Signal Publishers, 304 pp., $29, August 2026).

In a recent development, my holiday recommendation is Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick’s Israel’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power. Israel’s rightward shift, ever-expanding occupation, and Gaza genocide have produced a sea-change in U.S. attitudes toward Israel. Yet Democratic and Republican politicians continue to give Israel nearly unconditional support and diplomatic protection, even when Israel defies U.S. wishes or takes actions that harm U.S. interests. Clifton and Lustick explain this puzzle by showing how hard-line pro-Israel individuals and groups have taken advantage of the lax campaign financing rules created by the 2010 Citizens United decision to keep politicians on board.

Recent findings suggest that having lost the battle for public opinion, the Israel lobby now relies primarily on raw political muscle, mostly in the form of money. (The recent midterm elections suggest this tactic may be beginning to backfire). Clifton and Lustick also describe how Israel’s most ardent defenders have used false charges of antisemitism to silence criticism of Israel, which poses broader threats to freedom of speech. If you’re curious why the United States keeps landing in quagmires in the Middle East, this book provides part of the answer.

Roger Berkowitz (Yale University Press, 176 pp., $28, October 2026).

According to recent reports, at a time when political disagreement can be reason to end a friendship, Roger Berkowitz makes the case that democracy depends on our ability to nurture relationships across deep divides. In A World We Share, Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center at Bard College, offers an anatomy of Arendt’s friendships, which spanned fierce intellectual disagreements and profound moral differences.

According to recent reports, arendt’s circle included figures as disparate as the novelist Mary McCarthy, philosopher Karl Jaspers, and her one-time lover Martin Heidegger, whose embrace of Nazism tested the limits of a friendship with Arendt, a Jewish survivor of Adolf Hitler’s persecution. Berkowitz draws on Arendt’s extensive correspondence, including detailed epistolary exchanges on subjects as diverse as the Holocaust, Watergate, and marital infidelity. Through these relationships, Berkowitz makes the case that democracy depends upon worldviews grounded in mutual respect, spirited debate, and a willingness to break bread, exchange ideas, and forge emotional bonds with people whose convictions we reject.

Sources indicate that his argument speaks to a moment when ideological certainties and litmus tests increasingly crowd out curiosity, and political differences can eclipse our ability to see common humanity, much less make common cause. As our politics enters a newly introduced and more hopeful phase, and as families and friends gather at holiday tables, this timely book is an invitation to rediscover the democratic necessity of friendship across divides.

Sources indicate that C. Thi Nguyen (Penguin Press, 368 pp., $32, January 2026).

Industry observers note that the Score, by philosopher C. Thi Nguyen, is a love letter to games, but it is also a surprising treatise on bureaucracy. The book interrogates how so much of modern life has become an exercise of keeping score through data, metrics, and rankings. That focus on the quantitative, Nguyen argues, can produce beauty and fun in a game, yet it can warp behavior to disastrous effect everywhere else.

According to recent reports, in public policy, scorekeeping allows governments to create order and track progress in a sprawling, messy world, but often at the expense of context or nuance. Among Nguyen’s case studies is the work of anthropologist Sally Engle Merry on the U.S. State Department’s sex-trafficking report, which, by judging countries by their conviction rates, incentivized greater policing over reducing poverty.

For all its insights on processes and institutions, the book is also a joyous, sensual celebration of rock-climbing, fly-fishing, yo-yoing, and other pursuits that resist the gamification and optimization so characteristic of today’s world.

—Megan DuBois, associate editor.

Tareq Baconi (Washington Square Press, 256 pp., $19, October 2026, paperback).

It has been revealed that after I gifted Fire in Every Direction to a friend earlier this year, she sent me a message thanking me for the “novel”; she had read the first few pages and was immediately engrossed. Her misperception speaks to how engagingly Tareq Baconi narrates his own coming-of-age story—it reads like a bildungsroman, but it’s all true.

Baconi is a leading expert on Hamas, which he has previously written about for FP. In Fire in Every Direction, he takes a step back from his academic perch to reflect on his at-times painful journey to self-acceptance as a gay Palestinian man. Since his childhood in Amman, Jordan, Baconi had an intangible sense that he was different from his peers. His unrequited infatuation with a male classmate led to a broader reckoning within his family about sexuality and shame.

To escape Amman’s stifling conservatism, Baconi chose to attend university in London. Although there’s no love lost between him and Jordan—where his twice-displaced Palestinian parents begrudgingly fled to from Beirut during Lebanon’s civil war—he eventually finds his way back to Palestine. Rather than challenge his devotion to the Palestinian cause, Baconi’s queer identity affirms his commitment to securing liberation for all people.

Sources indicate that david M. Sacks (Henry Holt and Co., 528 pp., $36.99, November 2026).

It has been revealed that the Realist is a lucid, compelling, and granular biography of Hans Morgenthau, one of the most influential scholars of international politics in the immediate postwar era. David M. Sacks’ deft book provides a complete sweep of Morgenthau’s life and career from a small, provincial town in Germany to the global metropolis of New York.

Sources indicate that A German-Jewish émigré who had direct experience of the rising tides of vicious antisemitism, Morgenthau succeeded after tireless efforts to find a professorship at the University of Chicago. After an illustrious career, he moved to the City College of New York, where he quickly became a fixture of the city’s intellectual establishment. As a public intellectual, Morgenthau was also an early and vociferous critic of the Vietnam War, despite harboring a deep-seated hostility toward the Soviet Union.

Sonia Gandhi (Knopf, $28, 544 pp., November 2026).

Sonia Gandhi is one of the most fascinating living political leaders in South Asia, but also one of its least understood. She rose from humble beginnings in Italy to become the scion of India’s biggest family dynasty, even becoming linked with India’s independence (her late husband Rajiv was the grandson of the country’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru). But this remarkable life trajectory also led to great tragedy, due to the assassinations of her mother-in law, Indira, in 1984, and of Rajiv in 1991.

Gandhi, who turns 80 next month, has always been very private about her personal life and rarely opens up publicly. We haven’t had a true sense of her life and how it has shaped her. Belonging, her newly introduced memoir released earlier this month, tells a story that many in India and beyond have long wanted to hear.

—Michael Kugelman, FP’s South Asia Brief writer.

Saleem Haddad (Europa Editions, 336 pp., $19, February 2026).

One of the most memorable novels I read this year was Saleem Haddad’s Floodlines, a multigenerational epic that stretches from Baghdad to London and elsewhere between. The three Iraqi British sisters at its center—who are variously estranged—are pulled back together by the discovery of lost artwork by their late father, a renowned painter.

Recent findings suggest that the family that Haddad sketches feels real enough that a reader might be tricked into thinking the characters are loosely fictionalized. (The author drew on the story of his own great-uncle, an Iraqi modernist painter, for inspiration.) Even with elements of magical realism at play, Floodlines is ultimately rooted in the political and cultural history of Iraq.

It has been revealed that the book reaches its climax in 2014, with the Islamic State on the rise. As an unlikely plot brings its characters back home, Haddad manages to strike a genuine note of hope against a backdrop of conflict, exile, and rupture. And despite the family dysfunction driving it, Floodlines would make an excellent gift for a close relative or friend.

—Audrey Wilson, managing editor.

Roger Zakheim (Regnery History, 472 pp., $40, November 2026).

Most accounts of U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s foreign policy focus on his high-level summitry and arms control agreements with Soviet Premier Mikhail Gorbachev. But in Peace Through Strength, Roger Zakheim, the director of the Reagan Institute, tells the story of his military buildup. Zakheim argues that Reagan was able to sustain the largest peacetime military expansion in U.S. history across two presidential terms in the face of stiff opposition, even from his own party, because he saw it as essential to his Cold War strategy.

As the free world faces threats from a latest axis of aggressors, Trump calls for a record $1.5 trillion U.S. defense budget, and allied governments in NATO and the Indo-Pacific pledge to spend up to 5 percent of GDP on defense, democratic leaders are once again vexed by the question of how to maintain public and parliamentary support for a yearslong peacetime rearmament program. They would be well served to learn from Reagan’s successful example.

Catherine Liu (Verso, 192 pp., $24.95, September 2026).

I was inspired to read Catherine Liu’s Traumatized after Gregory Jones-Katz’s excellent review of the book in FP—and it was every bit as compelling as promised. Not since Lauren Berlant’s 2011 classic Cruel Optimism have I encountered such a thoughtful treatment of society’s obsession with trauma narratives and the ways they impede our understanding of, and appetite for, political change.

Liu, a cultural theorist at the University of California, Irvine, examines the ways that social media has amplified these narratives, which have come to pervade the political spectrum, contributing to, among other things, inequality, apathy, and the death of liberalism.

It’s not light reading, per se, but it’s provocative, elegantly written, and deeply relevant to our current moment.

Ryan Gingeras (Avid Reader Press / Simon & Schuster, 416 pp., $35, February 2026).

It has been revealed that here is the story of the 20th century told from the other side of the law. In Mafia, historian Ryan Gingeras shows how organized crime made the United States and how the United States in turn remade organized crime on a global scale through its economic might, law enforcement efforts, and popular culture. From early Balkan brigands through the last season of Narcos, this wide-ranging and fast-moving account takes readers on a journey through the dark shadows of globalization.

Mohammed Soliman (Polity, 272 pp., $24.95, February 2026).

In the Washington lexicon, the term “Middle East” often conjures up images of protracted wars, militant groups, and failed U.S. attempts at nation-building. In his fresh book, analyst Mohammed Soliman argues that moving past these quagmires requires reframing how the region is viewed entirely. Enter “West Asia,” a term that places the region at the edge of the world’s largest continent in lieu of its original Eurocentric conception.

Anchoring his thesis in the evolving ties among the wealthy Arab Gulf states, Israel, India, Egypt, and Japan—to name a few—Soliman argues that Washington should build a upcoming regional order connecting the old Middle East to the Indo-Pacific predicated on realpolitik, technology, and shared security incentives.

A caveat: The book was published weeks before the United States launched its protracted war against Iran, which has injected more uncertainty into the prospect of Soliman’s proposed order. But rather than negating the book’s thesis, the Iran war has only underscored the importance of a upcoming and provocative blueprint for what could come next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.

In keeping with tradition, President Donald Trump marked his sixth Thanksgiving in the executive office with the White House’s annual Turkey Pardon ceremony on Tuesday.

His plans for Thanksgiving Day this year remain unannounced — but previous holidays offer a preview of how the president likes to spend the day honoring those who can't be at home for the uniquely American holiday due to service to the country.

According to recent reports, last year, Trump spent Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago participating in his favorite pastime — golf. But he also used the time in what is known as the "Winter White House" to call Maj. Gen. Dave Gardner, commander of the 101st Airborne Division and Joint Task Force–Southern Border, by video conference and talk with troops deployed along the southern border.

TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. troops in an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst).

First lady Melania Trump spent the days ahead of the holiday in 2025 visiting Camp Lejeune and Marine Corps Air Station Newly introduced River with second lady Usha Vance on Nov. 19. They met with military families and made Thanksgiving crafts with children.

In 2020, during the final Thanksgiving of his first term, Trump remained at the White House and made calls to six deployed military units representing every branch of the armed forces, including troops in Kuwait and sailors aboard the USS Winston Churchill in the Red Sea.

Trump famously took a secret trip to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, which not even two years later, in August 2021, was brought to an end by then-President Joe Biden.

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time.

"And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you.".

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet military personnel during an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst).

TRUMP CLAIMS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN.

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

Recent findings suggest that during the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He mentioned his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump visits with personnel at U.S. Coast Guard Station Lake Worth Inlet in Riviera Beach, Florida, on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 22, 2018. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images).

Trump spent Thanksgiving 2018 in Florida having a traditional dinner with his family, including Melania and his children and grandchildren.

He also held a video call with deployed troops before visiting Coast Guard members at Station Lake Worth Inlet with his wife, where the first couple thanked them for their service and hurricane rescues.

After that holiday in 2018, Melania and then-second lady Karen Pence assembled comfort kits for deployed troops at American Red Cross headquarters.

It’s Time to Settle With Russia

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
